metadata.title: PISA Data Analysis Manual: SPSS, Second Edition (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The manual describes PISA’s two-stage sampling (schools then students within schools) and explains that analyses must use the provided student final weights to obtain unbiased population estimates. It specifies the student final weight variable W_FSTUWT and notes that weights are also associated with schools, with non-response adjustments and oversampling of explicit strata for national reporting. For standard errors, the manual requires replicate-based variance estimation (Fay’s BRR replicates) because students within the same school are not independent under the complex design. It also documents a practical shortcut for exploratory work: normalising weights so their sum matches the unweighted sample size, and optionally applying design effects when replicates are skipped; however, it advises using replicates for final reporting.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is an official IEA/OECD technical report or assessment framework. It describes sampling, scaling, and instrument design rather than student-level predictive modeling. Plausible values are therefore not applicable to the document's primary analytic purpose; any missing-data discussion refers to fieldwork or scaling procedures, not a single ML imputation strategy.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The manual’s worked multilevel example uses PISA 2006 science performance data with 387,769 students from 14,052 schools in 55 countries/economies. It describes that the PISA international database includes all students who attended assessment sessions, plus questionnaire-only students if they provided at least one student questionnaire response and parental occupation is known; it excludes students reported as not eligible, no longer at school, excluded for physical/mental/linguistic reasons, absent on testing day, refused participation, and students from schools where <25% of sampled eligible non-excluded students participated. For the multilevel regression example, missing values were handled via a missing-dummy approach with imputation for individual and school-level predictors (system-level variables were not imputed due to small n=55), and variables were recoded where necessary; France and Qatar were not included in the HLM example.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD manual documents how to analyse PISA data correctly under the programme’s complex survey design and plausible-values framework. It explains that PISA uses a two-stage sampling process (schools, then students within schools), which increases standard errors relative to simple random sampling; therefore, analysts must use the provided student final weights (W_FSTUWT) and replicate weights (80 Fay’s BRR replicates) to compute unbiased sampling variance estimates. For achievement outcomes, PISA reports performance using plausible values: analyses should be run separately on five plausible values per student and then aggregated to combine sampling and imputation error. The manual also provides guidance on missing data handling for modelling examples, using a missing-dummy approach and imputation for individual/school-level predictors while not imputing system-level variables when the number of systems is small. It further describes the PISA 2006 rotated test design and the structure of the international database, including questionnaire instruments and available weights/replicates.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This document is a methodological manual/data documentation for PISA analysis rather than an empirical ML study with a predictive target and reported model performance. As such, it does not estimate ML models or report outcome effects; instead, it specifies recommended procedures (weights, replicates, plausible values) and provides worked examples of how to implement them. Consequently, fields related to ML techniques and main findings are intentionally empty, while survey design and PV/missing-data handling are the substantive content.
